extracted.intended_audience: readers of socio-economic theory; economists, sociologists, and educated general readers interested in Veblen's critique of leisure-class institutions
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter excerpt from Thorstein Veblen's The Theory of the Leisure Class discussing the social norms, economic effects, and justificatory rhetoric around sports, conspicuous leisure, gambling, and the 'belief in luck'. It analyzes how leisure-class canons shape what is 'decorous' and the tension with the instinct of workmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canon of reputable living / conspicuous leisure
rubrics_metrics.description: The canons of reputable living exclude from the scheme of life of the leisure class all activity that cannot be classed as conspicuous leisure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Activities deemed decorous must visibly signify non-productivity; social prestige is attached to occupations and habits that advertise exemption from useful effort. Examples: walking-stick as an advertisement of unused hands. Anti-pattern: doing useful or serviceable work is socially discreditable for the leisure class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leisure-class canon of reputable waste
rubrics_metrics.description: To be decorous an employment must conform to the leisure-class canon of reputable waste; the leisure-class canon demands strict and comprehensive futility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legitimately 'leisure' occupations should be wasteful in an ostentatious way. The canon acts by selectively eliminating substantially useful modes of action from accredited life. Anti-pattern: occupations exhibiting clear serviceability are excluded from being considered decorous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports must combine substantial futility with colorable purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Sports satisfy requirements of substantial futility together with a colorable make-believe of purpose; they provide proximate unreflected purposefulness while remaining ultimately futile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A recreation that appears to have an immediate, unreflected purpose (dexterity, emulation) can be sustained as decorous even though it is ultimately purposeless. This proximate purposefulness appeases the instinct of workmanship in persons lacking reflection. Anti-pattern: purposeless activity with no pretense of purpose fails to pass as decorous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope for emulation as a criterion of recreational value
rubrics_metrics.description: Recreations are attractive and decorous to the leisure class insofar as they afford scope for emulation and expression of dominance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Activities that permit emulative rivalry and public display of prowess are socially prized. Sports are therefore preferred because they allow exhibition of ferocity and astuteness. Anti-pattern: solitary or non-competitive exercise lacks the emulative element and is less valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tension between instinct of workmanship and leisure-canon
rubrics_metrics.description: The instinct of workmanship demands purposeful action for serviceable ends, whereas the leisure-class canon demands futility; legitimacy of an activity depends on reconciling proximate purposefulness with ulterior futility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An activity persists as habitual expression only if attention can be confined to proximate purposes to avoid organismal revulsion at ulterior futility. Evaluations should note how activities manage this tension. Anti-pattern: activities that expose their ulterior futility to reflective agents will be resisted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification of athletics by claimed developmental benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocates commonly justify athletic games by claiming they improve physique and foster a manly spirit in participants and spectators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This justificatory strategy is often invoked to legitimize sports despite their predatory aspects, but the author notes the chain of proof from sports to genuine 'workmanship' is often weak or incomplete. Anti-pattern: asserting development benefits without clear causal evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of selection and discipline for sporting serviceability
rubrics_metrics.description: Serviceability for lusory institutions requires sedulous training or breeding; material (human or brute) is selected and disciplined to accentuate ferine aptitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The cultivation of sporting skills tends to produce a one-sided rehabilitation of ferine traits (ferocity, cunning) without corresponding traits for self-preservation in a ferine environment. Implication: measure sporting training not by all-around usefulness but by its role in accentuating specific competitive aptitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of predatory traits: individual advantage vs collective disutility
rubrics_metrics.description: Ferocity and cunning cultivated by sports are advantageous to individuals in competitive contexts but are of little or no direct use to the community (except in hostile dealings with other communities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate traits by their economic bearing on collective life: traits that help individual emulative success may not further collective adjustment to environment; record whether benefits are primarily private or public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency of sports to foster fraud and chicanery
rubrics_metrics.description: Strategy and cunning in games tend to develop into finesse and chicanery; fraudulent practices and attempts to overreach opponents are not adventitious but habitual within games.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of technical regulations and umpires attests to accepted limits of permissible fraud; nonetheless habituation to such practices can increase aptitude for sharp practice in broader economic life. Anti-pattern: treating these practices as merely incidental rather than structurally fostered by competitive games.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of status signals to advertise non-productivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects or habits of polite usage (e.g., carrying a walking-stick) function as advertisements that the bearer's hands are employed otherwise than in useful effort and thus evidence leisure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret status signals as dual-purpose: they mark exemption from useful labor while sometimes also serving predatory comfort (walking-stick as weapon). When analysing social practice, note both symbolic and practical facets of such signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for legitimating predatory institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Because predatory habits (sports, exploit) are presumptively incompatible with collective economic ends, the burden of proof lies with those who rehabilitate such practices to show they foster workmanship or social utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apologetic discourse often piles up assertions without rigorous causal demonstration; evaluators should demand clear empirical or theoretical linkage showing how predatory practices convert into socially serviceable dispositions. Anti-pattern: reliance on emotive asseveration in place of causal proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief in luck (gambler's animism) as economically deleterious
rubrics_metrics.description: The belief in luck underlies the gambling propensity; it is an archaic animistic/preternatural sense that events possess propensities and can be propitiated, and is inimical to modern industrial efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish the two elements of the belief in luck: an incipient animism attributing quasi-personal propensities to objects, and a later phase positing a preternatural agency that can be influenced. Evaluate gambling not only as individual pastime but as a social habit that undermines rational, industrial conduct. Note also the ancillary motive of using wagers to strengthen a favored contestant's chances (partisan backing).
